bottlenecks.name: Aerothermal environment: laminar-turbulent transition, shock-boundary-layer interaction (SBLI), gap and cavity heating
bottlenecks.description: Predicting where the boundary layer turns turbulent and how much heat shock interactions (flaps, hinge lines, tile steps and gaps) deposit. Turbulent heating runs roughly 3-5x laminar (general), so unpredictable transition forces designers to assume early or fully turbulent flow. RANS models fail on hypersonic SBLI: they mispredict separation and the joint heat-flux/shear signature (Raje et al., arXiv 2412.13985 v2, Apr 2025). Predicting transition on complex 3D geometry is still the subject of a coordinated international effort (AIAA virtual collection, Mar 2026), and BOLT-1B (Mach 7.2) confirmed that flight transition behaves differently from wind-tunnel transition (JHU APL, Jan 2026).
bottlenecks.ondemand_math_help: Mixed. Solved in principle but expert-scarce: 3D linear and nonlinear stability analysis (PSE, plane-marching PSE, resolvent/input-output), setup of wall-modeled LES and DNS, gap-heating analysis. A few specialist groups worldwide do these, taking months per vehicle; an on-demand AI unlock (P1) would make them routine by 2027-28 in S2. Genuinely open: receptivity to the flight disturbance environment, transition induced by roughness or ablation, and non-Boussinesq SBLI heat-flux closures. AI can propose theory for these, but flight and quiet-tunnel data gate validation.

bottlenecks.name: Thermochemical nonequilibrium and radiative heating (Mars/Venus CO2 entries, Earth return at 11-14 km/s)
bottlenecks.description: Shock-layer chemistry and radiation set the heating for fast entries. For the 8 km/s Mars Sample Retrieval Lander (SRL) entry, radiation exceeded the convective heating of MSL. Baseline models under-predicted vacuum-ultraviolet (VUV) emission by up to 2x against NASA's EAST shock tube, and three uncertainty-quantification methods gave radiative-heating uncertainties between 30% and 100% (Hansson, RHTGSM workshop, 24 Sep 2026). For Earth return at ~12 km/s, heating exceeds 3,000 W/cm2 and radiation becomes a first-order load (ESA).
bottlenecks.ondemand_math_help: AI can build state-resolved excitation and dissociation kinetics from ab initio potential surfaces and shock-tube data, then reduce them to engineering models with error bounds. This is partly open physics (heavy-particle excitation was the missing term at SRL) and partly expensive expert work. Family 275 (QMA-hardness of continuum Coulomb energies, T1) is a ceiling: no general exact first-principles shortcut exists. EAST shot rate is the physical gate.

bottlenecks.name: Material response: ablation, pyrolysis, gas-surface interaction, char failure, reusable tile durability
bottlenecks.description: Material-property uncertainty dominates TPS thickness. In NASA's SRL design, PICA-D conductivity carries a 2-sigma uncertainty of about 32% and the material margin dominates the RSS thickness (Alpert et al., IPPW 2026). Failure modes escape the models. Artemis I's Avcoat char loss came from insufficient permeability, and finding it took 121 tests across 8 campaigns (NASA). Recession models such as PATO match plasma-tunnel data to about +/-20% (ESA conference, 2026). For reusable tiles (Starship, ~18,000 tiles), the problem is cracking, edge damage, hot-gas ingress at tile boundaries and bond fatigue across flights (Flight 13 reporting, Jul-Aug 2026).
bottlenecks.ondemand_math_help: Homogenization from pore scale to volume average, inverse calibration of properties from arc-jet data, and failure criteria are partly open and largely expert-scarce. Inverse-problem theory for inspection gets a direct boost from catalog families 365 (T3), 372 (T1) and 366 (T1). The physical gate is arc-jet hours: the Ames Arc Jet Complex is NASA's only ground facility for reentry TPS testing. Reflight count gates reusable-tile models.

bottlenecks.name: Margins, uncertainty quantification and ground-to-flight extrapolation
bottlenecks.description: Designers stack deterministic factors. For SRL: a convective heat-flux factor of 1.22 forebody and 2.0 aftbody, radiative 1.5 and 1.47, a 20% recession margin, and a bondline margin. NASA's own alternative-margining study shows that a heat shield at ~75% of baseline thickness still gives 99% confidence that the bondline stays below its allowable (Alpert et al., IPPW 2026). Model-form error in extrapolating from arc-jet to flight is the genuinely hard part.
bottlenecks.ondemand_math_help: Mostly solved in principle but expert-scarce: joint probabilistic margins, reliability-based sizing, Bayesian optimal experimental design and model-form error bounds. This is the fastest AI unlock in the domain (P1, then P5). It is gated by adoption: program margin policy and the risk culture after Artemis I.

bottlenecks.name: EDL guidance and powered descent: supersonic retropropulsion, aerocapture guidance, precision landing
bottlenecks.description: All of NASA's 20 t human-scale Mars lander concepts rely on supersonic retropropulsion (NASA EDL Architecture Study). The interaction between plume and freestream is unsteady and hard to test at scale on Earth. Aerocapture has never flown: NASA is studying an Earth demonstration, including a $350k Inversion study through June 2027 (Sep 2026), and Uranus studies find MSL-heritage aeroshells adequate but require a risk-reduction flight demo first.
bottlenecks.ondemand_math_help: Guidance with proofs (convex powered-descent guidance, robust predictor-corrector aerocapture guidance) is formal-verification work: P2, gated by qualification. Aero-propulsive SRP models are applied-math work gated by data, since full-scale flight data comes only from Falcon 9 and Starship and is proprietary.

bottlenecks.name: Rarefied, kinetic and plasma effects: DSMC versus Boltzmann, high-altitude aerocapture passes, RF blackout
bottlenecks.description: DSMC codes (SPARTA and others) are the workhorse for transitional flow, with Fokker-Planck variants now cheaper. Rarefied heating matters most for aerocapture and early entry. Blackout is a coupled problem of nonequilibrium ionization and electromagnetics. Starship relays telemetry through Starlink, and magnetic windows remain at the screening-model stage (Lieu, arXiv 2608.10018, Aug 2026).
bottlenecks.ondemand_math_help: Families 363 (nonuniqueness) and 364 (kinetic limit with fluctuations) are manuscript-only (T1). If they hold, they change confidence in kinetic models and mark where a selection principle is needed. They change no numbers. Error-controlled hybrid kinetic solvers and coupled EM-plasma link analysis are expert-scarce engineering math that AI could make routine.

nodes.title: High-cadence instrumented reentry flights
nodes.description: A steady stream of instrumented hypersonic and orbital-reentry flights (Varda W-series, Talon-A, MACH-TB, Starship, Inversion Arc), whose surface heating, pressure and in-depth TPS temperatures reach model builders. Defined as achieved at 12 or more instrumented reentries per year with reconstructed data usable for calibration.
nodes.status_oct2026: Varda W-5 reentered on 29 Jan 2026 under the AFRL Prometheus program with an in-house C-PICA heat shield. W-6 (launched 30 Mar 2026) carried a Sandia nose tile with embedded sensors for comparison against model predictions. Varda says it expects a monthly cadence. MACH-TB targets up to 50 tests a year, and Talon-A has flown more than 10 hypersonic flights. DoD describes test capacity as a national bottleneck across ~70 hypersonic programs.
nodes.why: Every AI-built aerothermal or material model in this tree has to be calibrated against flight data, because ground facilities cannot reproduce the combined flight environment. Flight count grows roughly linearly, from a few to tens per year, set by rideshare cadence and capital rather than by cognition. That makes this node the slope limiter for every data-bound node downstream, in all three scenarios.
nodes.strongest_case_small: Much of the best data is classified (defense hypersonics) or proprietary (SpaceX) and never reaches civil model builders. Cadence claims for commercial capsules have slipped before.
nodes.signpost: Varda, Inversion or AFRL publish reconstructed flight heating data; MACH-TB passes 20 flights in FY2027.

nodes.title: Boltzmann foundations checked and scoped
nodes.description: Outside experts check and scope family 363 (Boltzmann solutions that conserve mass, momentum and energy exactly yet are non-unique) and family 364 (Boltzmann derived from Newtonian hard-sphere gases, including fluctuations over the Boltzmann lifespan). The scoping should state whether the non-unique solutions satisfy the entropy inequality and whether they can occur at flight conditions.
nodes.status_oct2026: Both families are manuscript-only (T1): no Lean proof in the repo and no outside review as of 2026-10-07. The analyst knowledge base rates the implications for rarefied modeling as Low.
nodes.why: If 363 holds, the kinetic equation alone does not fix the physical solution in some regime, so DSMC and deterministic Boltzmann solvers need an explicit selection principle there (entropy, molecular chaos). If 364 holds, the particle-noise statistics of DSMC have a rigorous basis rather than being numerical artifacts. Both change confidence in the models, not the heating numbers. Band: P3 defaults to High, down one for the T1 premise in S1. In S2 and S3, cheap verification makes an expert check within 1-2 years likely.
nodes.strongest_case_small: Nonuniqueness constructions are usually low-regularity solutions that violate the H-theorem or need contrived data. DSMC has matched flight and tunnel data for decades, and no reentry heating number will change.
nodes.signpost: Kinetic-theory specialists publicly endorse or refute 363 within 12 months, especially on whether the counterexamples are entropy-admissible.

nodes.title: On-demand transition stability analysis for any vehicle
nodes.description: AI agents set up and run linear and nonlinear stability analyses (PSE, plane-marching PSE, resolvent/input-output, BiGlobal) on full 3D vehicle geometries with thermochemistry. They return N-factor maps and sensitivities to roughness and wall temperature in days rather than expert-months.
nodes.status_oct2026: The methods exist but only a few groups can apply them. BOLT-1B was analyzed by specialist teams using stochastically forced DNS and plane-marching PSE. The AIAA collection on transition prediction for complex geometry appeared in Mar 2026. LLM agents already automate routine CFD: OpenFOAMGPT 2.0 reports more than 450 end-to-end runs, but none for hypersonic stability.
nodes.why: Today a 3D stability analysis of a new vehicle takes a specialist team weeks to months (general), so most design iterations fall back on correlations (Re_theta/M_e). Once the expert labor is near-free (S2 from ~2027-28), each design iteration can carry a physics-based transition estimate, which is 10-50x more stability analyses for the same budget (judgment). P1 defaults to High. S1 is Medium because applied-math capability arrives later and diffuses slowly.
nodes.strongest_case_small: Stability theory gives N-factors, not a transition location. The critical N-factor and receptivity still have to be calibrated against flight, so the bottleneck moves to data rather than disappearing. Defense users may not run ITAR-controlled geometry through external AI services.
nodes.signpost: A published 3D hypersonic stability analysis set up end-to-end by an AI agent and validated against BOLT-1B or HIFiRE-5 data.

nodes.title: Information-optimal ground and flight test design
nodes.description: Bayesian optimal experimental design and sequential model calibration choose arc-jet conditions, shock-tube shots and flight sensor placements. Each test is aimed at the uncertainties that drive TPS thickness: material conductivity, radiative excitation rates and the transition N-factor.
nodes.status_oct2026: The methods are known but rarely applied at program scale. The Ames Arc Jet Complex is NASA's only reentry TPS ground facility, and its throughput is limited: in 2026 the 30 kW mARC II needed a cooling-sleeve fix just to extend run times. The Artemis I char-loss investigation took 121 tests across 8 campaigns.
nodes.why: When facility hours are the binding constraint, the lever is information gained per run. Well-designed sequential calibration campaigns often cut the runs needed for parameter estimation by 2-5x (general). Applied to the arc-jet and EAST queues, this multiplies the one physical gate in the domain that money cannot expand quickly. It also makes the tier-3 physics nodes reachable sooner.
nodes.strongest_case_small: Qualification requirements (envelope coverage) often fix test matrices, not information value, and facility availability sets the schedule. The real gain may be 20-30%, not 2-5x.
nodes.signpost: NASA Ames, ESA or a commercial plasma-tunnel operator advertises adaptive, model-driven test campaigns.

nodes.title: Probabilistic margins with model-form error bounds
nodes.description: Stacked deterministic multipliers are replaced by a joint probabilistic budget that carries material, aerothermal and model-form uncertainty through to a reliability statement on bondline temperature. Where data are sparse, the budget has rigorous bounds.
nodes.status_oct2026: NASA's SRL TPS design (IPPW 2026) uses stacked factors: convective 1.22 forebody and 2.0 aftbody, radiative 1.5 and 1.47, recession +20%, bondline margin. Material properties dominate the thickness. The same study's alternative margining gives ~75% of baseline thickness at 99% confidence on bondline temperature.
nodes.why: Stacking factors compounds conservatism, and NASA's own SRL numbers imply roughly a quarter of the thickness is margin on margin. Joint UQ is solved in principle but expert-scarce. Model-form error for extrapolating from ground to flight is genuinely open, and an AI doing research-grade applied math can attack it on demand. This is the shortest path from AI mathematics to mass on a flown vehicle.
nodes.strongest_case_small: The mathematics was never the barrier; risk posture is. Probabilistic TPS methods have existed for about 20 years (general), and Artemis I's char loss pushes NASA toward more margin, not less.
nodes.signpost: A NASA or ESA EDL margin-policy revision, or a mission PDR, that cites reliability-based TPS sizing.

nodes.title: Certified error bounds for hypersonic CFD kernels
nodes.description: Proven a-posteriori error bounds and formally verified kernels (positivity-preserving shock capturing, stiff finite-rate chemistry integrators, radiation-transport quadrature). A predicted stagnation heat flux then carries a certified numerical-error bar, kept separate from physics-model error.
nodes.status_oct2026: The release does not touch this: stiff numerics and radiation transport are absent, and only 3 of 16 PDE families are formalized. Practitioners study grid convergence informally, and it enters radiative-heating uncertainty budgets as a 'structural' term.
nodes.why: Separating numerical error from model error stops grid effects from being double-counted inside physics margins. In S2, Mathlib coverage of PDE and numerics (~2028) plus a verified-numerics toolchain (~2029) make kernel-level proofs routine. Proofs about the full solution remain out of reach.
nodes.strongest_case_small: Numerical error is rarely the dominant uncertainty; transition, radiation and material properties are. Multi-D compressible Euler weak solutions are known to be non-unique, so global certified bounds need assumptions engineers cannot check.
nodes.signpost: A Lean- or Coq-verified flux or chemistry integrator adopted in a NASA, DLR or commercial production aerothermal code.

nodes.title: Error-controlled kinetic solvers for the rarefied-to-continuum gap
nodes.description: Hybrids of DSMC, Fokker-Planck and discrete-velocity methods, with proven consistency with the Boltzmann equation and quantified statistical error, used for high-altitude aerocapture passes, early-entry heating and plume backflow.
nodes.status_oct2026: DSMC (SPARTA and other codes) is standard practice, and a Fokker-Planck module in SPARTA matches DSMC at lower cost. No production solver carries certified error bounds. Families 363 and 364 are manuscript-only (T1).
nodes.premise_tier: n/a (capability-driven; 363/364 at T1 are supporting only)
nodes.why: Transitional-regime heating (Knudsen number ~0.01-1) matters most for aerocapture, which spends a long time high in the atmosphere, and for upper-atmosphere entry. Today it is DSMC with expert-tuned collision models. The band rests on the capability channel. If it rested only on the T1 catalog premises, it would drop a band.
nodes.strongest_case_small: Rarefied contributions to total heat load are small for most capsules, because peak heating occurs in the continuum (general). Certified bounds also do nothing about collision cross-section uncertainty.
nodes.signpost: A kinetic code release with published, proven error estimates, or AI-derived collision models validated against shock-tube data.

nodes.title: Inverse-problem theory and algorithms for heat-shield inspection
nodes.description: Uniqueness and stability theory, plus algorithms, for recovering hidden TPS defects (bondline disbonds, subsurface cracks, density variation) from surface thermography, ultrasound and strain data. This includes which defects a given sensing mode provably cannot see.
nodes.status_oct2026: Family 372 (global uniqueness for smooth isotropic elasticity from boundary data) is T1. Family 365 (joint metric and connection recovery from one boundary patch, plus conductivity nonuniqueness) is T3, Lean-formalized and unchecked. Family 366 (planar Mumford-Shah crack regularity) is T1. Practice relies on visual, tap and thermographic inspection with empirical thresholds. Starship's heat shield has about 18,000 tiles; Musk has described the job as inspecting tens of thousands of tiles.
nodes.premise_tier: T1-T3 (supportive; the capability channel drives the band)
nodes.why: Rapid reuse needs inspect-by-exception: cheap sensors that show which tiles need attention. Uniqueness results say when boundary data determines interior properties. The conductivity nonuniqueness in 365 says thermal boundary data alone can miss some interior variations, which is a fast-acting P3 design rule: pair thermography with a second modality. AI also makes the bespoke inversion work, such as probability-of-detection modeling for a specific tile stack, cheap.
nodes.strongest_case_small: These theorems concern smooth, isotropic media, while tiles are porous, anisotropic and full of sharp interfaces. Industrial NDE runs on empirical probability-of-detection curves, and SpaceX will use cameras plus machine learning regardless.
nodes.signpost: A reusable-vehicle operator or NASA publishes a model-based TPS inspection scheme with probability-of-detection derived from inverse theory.

nodes.title: Predictive hypersonic transition (receptivity, roughness, ablation)
nodes.description: A validated model that predicts transition onset on 3D vehicles from the freestream disturbance environment, surface roughness and ablation blowing, to within ~+/-20% in transition Reynolds number, without per-vehicle tuning.
nodes.status_oct2026: Genuinely open. A coordinated international effort was published as an AIAA virtual collection in Mar 2026. BOLT-1B showed that flight transition differs from conventional-tunnel transition (Jan 2026), and its forebody took ~14 months and 100+ staff to build.
nodes.why: Turbulent heating is roughly 3-5x laminar (general), so without trusted transition prediction, slender and lifting vehicles carry TPS sized for turbulent flow over much of their acreage. Predictive transition could save tens of percent of acreage TPS mass on such vehicles (judgment). Under S2, AI can produce the theory by 2029-30. Validation needs flight transition datasets, of which there are only a handful (BOLT, HIFiRE), and the flight disturbance environment is poorly characterized. The physical clock keeps S2 at Low.
nodes.strongest_case_small: Blunt capsules and Starship's belly transition early anyway, and designs already assume turbulent heating. The payoff falls mainly on hypersonic gliders and weapons, not most space vehicles.
nodes.signpost: A blind prediction in which an AI-assisted model lands transition onset on a new flight test within 20%.

nodes.title: Turbulence closures for shock interactions and cold-wall heating
nodes.description: AI-derived RANS and wall-model closures (non-Boussinesq, variable turbulent Prandtl number, roughness and blowing) that predict separation extent and peak heating in shock-boundary-layer interactions (flaps, control surfaces, tile steps and gaps) to within ~+/-15-20% of DNS and experiment.
nodes.status_oct2026: Standard RANS fails on hypersonic SBLI. The 2025 review by Raje, Parish, Hickey, Cinnella and Duraisamy lists SBLI heat transfer, compressibility, turbulence-chemistry interaction and ablation roughness and blowing as open research needs. The release contains no turbulence-closure results.
nodes.why: Flap, hinge-line and gap heating set the local TPS on Starship-class flaps and control surfaces, which today are designed with LES or DNS spot checks plus factors. Deriving closures is a theory problem that AI can attack (constraint-respecting symbolic models trained on DNS) once enough DNS data exists. DNS is compute-bound, and AI-era compute growth helps. In S2 the cognitive part lands by ~2029, and data and validation take about another year.
nodes.strongest_case_small: Machine-learned RANS closures have repeatedly failed to generalize outside their training data (general). Wall-modeled LES on GPUs may bypass RANS closures by 2030 and make the question moot.
nodes.signpost: A closure published with demonstrated out-of-distribution accuracy on unseen SBLI geometries in a blind comparison.

nodes.title: Closing the radiative-heating gap (Mars, Venus, 12+ km/s return)
nodes.description: State-resolved excitation and dissociation kinetics (the CO 4th positive system in CO2 atmospheres; N and O VUV emission for Earth return), built from ab initio rates plus shock-tube data, that cut radiative-heating uncertainty from 30-100% to ~15-25%.
nodes.status_oct2026: For SRL's 8 km/s Mars entry, baseline simulations under-predicted VUV by up to 2x against EAST, and three UQ methods gave 30-100% uncertainty (Hansson, 24 Sep 2026). The forebody radiative heating factor is 1.5. Family 275 (QMA-hardness of continuum Coulomb energies, T1) acts as a ceiling on first-principles shortcuts.
nodes.premise_tier: n/a (capability-driven; 275 at T1 is a ceiling only)
nodes.why: Radiative uncertainty sets the 1.5x factor on Mars forebody radiative heating. For Earth return at 12 km/s or more, radiation dominates and the uncertainty decides material choice (HEEET-class versus PICA). Halving the uncertainty could bring the factor toward ~1.2-1.25 and cut the radiative design heat load by ~15-20% (judgment). AI can generate rate sets and reduced kinetics, but the missing physics at SRL (heavy-particle excitation) was found by measurement, and EAST shot rate binds.
nodes.strongest_case_small: The gap is experimental, not theoretical, and 275 says no general exact shortcut exists for the many-electron energies behind those rates. The best AI theory still needs shock-tube shots that take months to schedule.
nodes.signpost: A paper at a radiation workshop (RHTGSM or IPPW) in which AI-generated rate sets match EAST VUV spectra within 20% without tuning.

nodes.title: First-principles gas-surface chemistry for heat-shield materials
nodes.description: Finite-rate oxidation, nitridation and catalytic-recombination models for carbon, SiC and silica-based (tile coating) surfaces, derived from quantum chemistry plus molecular-beam data, to replace tuned recession and catalycity parameters.
nodes.status_oct2026: Finite-rate models exist, for example vitreous-carbon oxidation mechanisms extended to FiberForm (the PICA precursor), but they rely on fitted mechanisms. Family 278 (failure of Kohn-Sham ensemble representability, T1) marks cases where DFT can be formally underdetermined. Family 275 (T1) is a complexity ceiling.
nodes.premise_tier: n/a (capability-driven; 278/275 at T1 are ceilings only)
nodes.why: On reusable, non-ablating tiles, surface catalycity can shift heating by tens of percent up to ~2x between the non-catalytic and fully catalytic limits (general), so designers assume the worst case. Recession-rate uncertainty sets the 20% recession margin on ablators. AI-built mechanisms validated by autonomous molecular-beam and plasma-tunnel experiments (S2 from ~2029) could tighten both.
nodes.strongest_case_small: Real surfaces evolve through contamination, oxide growth and microstructure change, so first-principles rates are only one input. Arc-jet calibration remains mandatory, and arc jets are scarce.
nodes.signpost: Autonomous plasma-tunnel or molecular-beam experiments publish AI-designed reaction mechanisms that predict catalytic heating within 20% on a new material.

nodes.title: Predictive ablator response (pyrolysis, permeability, spallation)
nodes.description: Multiscale material response that goes from pore scale to volume average, with mathematically justified homogenization, calibrated permeability and pyrolysis kinetics, and criteria for spallation and char failure. It should be able to predict an Avcoat-type char loss before flight.
nodes.status_oct2026: PATO recession predictions match plasma-tunnel data to about +/-20% (ESA conference, 2026). The Artemis I char-loss root cause (Avcoat lacking permeability, letting gas pressure build in the char) was found only after flight, through 121 tests. Artemis II splashed down on 10 Apr 2026 after a modified, non-skip entry, with reduced char loss on the same heat-shield design.
nodes.why: Material-property uncertainty dominates TPS thickness (SRL: conductivity 2-sigma ~32%). A failure mode the models missed cost Artemis a trajectory change and an investigation of more than a year. An AI that formulates and checks thermomechanical failure criteria from micro-CT microstructure addresses the cognitive part. Validation needs arc-jet time, which in S2 is stretched by optimal test design.
nodes.strongest_case_small: Batch-to-batch permeability in Avcoat is a manufacturing process-control problem, and better models do not make material uniform.
nodes.signpost: A pre-test prediction of a char or spallation anomaly that arc-jet or flight data later confirms.

nodes.title: Damage-accumulation model for reusable ceramic tiles
nodes.description: A predictive model of tile cracking, edge chipping, bond fatigue and hot-gas ingress through gaps over repeated entries, tied to inspection data, so that operators can inspect by exception and set life limits per tile zone.
nodes.status_oct2026: Starship V3 Flight 13 (24-25 Jul 2026) deliberately stressed the heat shield: minimal tile loss, but cracked tiles and streaks at tile boundaries that suggest hot-gas penetration. Load-sensing tiles were flown and reflown tiles were tested. Musk said on 4 Aug 2026 that he would call the heat shield problem solved. Dan Rasky (co-inventor of PICA) called the current TPS a dead end for rapid reuse (29 Jul 2026). Flight 14 reached orbit on 28 Sep 2026 and splashed down; no ship has been caught or reflown.
nodes.why: Shuttle-era tile programs needed extensive inspection between flights (general). Rapid reuse at Starship scale needs model-based triage that narrows inspection to flagged zones, plausibly a few percent of tiles per flight (judgment). Fatigue and fracture modeling plus Bayesian updating from load-sensing tiles is expert-scarce applied math that AI makes cheap. The data clock is the number of reflights.
nodes.strongest_case_small: SpaceX would build this anyway with in-house ML on inspection imagery, and AI mathematics adds at most a few months. The hard problem may be material (ceramic tile fatigue under thermal cycling), and no model removes that.
nodes.signpost: SpaceX states a ship reflight with heat-shield turnaround under 2 weeks, or publishes tile life-limit data.

nodes.title: AI-run aerothermal design loop (shape + trajectory + TPS)
nodes.description: Multi-fidelity co-optimization of vehicle shape, entry trajectory and TPS layout, using AI-built surrogates (neural fields, reduced-order models) with validated or certified error bars. It cuts an entry-vehicle design cycle from months to days.
nodes.status_oct2026: Surrogates exist in research: physics-enhanced 3D neural fields for Orion (arXiv 2603.28791, Mar 2026), and LLM CFD agents (OpenFOAMGPT 2.0, CFDAgent) that automate setup. None is used in production for certified EDL design.
nodes.why: Entry design iterates between aerodynamics, trajectory and TPS, and each loop needs nonequilibrium CFD at 10-100 trajectory points (general). Agents plus surrogates could compress a cycle 10-30x (judgment). That opens shapes that were too costly to explore, such as lifting bodies and biconic Mars landers, and lowers the analysis-cost barrier for small companies (see the aerocapture demo).
nodes.strongest_case_small: Design-cycle time is rarely on a program's critical path; test and fabrication are. Neural surrogates struggle with shocks and extrapolation, and high-consequence final designs will still need full CFD plus test.
nodes.signpost: A NASA or commercial entry-vehicle design review that cites trade studies driven by AI surrogates.

nodes.title: Probabilistic heat-shield sizing adopted in practice
nodes.description: A NASA program, an ESA mission or a commercial capsule maker formally sizes heat-shield thickness to a reliability target using joint probabilistic margins rather than stacked factors.
nodes.status_oct2026: Shown only as an alternative-margining study for SRL (~75% of baseline thickness at 99% confidence on bondline temperature; IPPW 2026). The SRL baseline still stacks factors. Varda makes its C-PICA heat shields in-house and flies roughly quarterly, aiming for monthly.
nodes.why: Applying SRL's ~25% thickness reduction where forebody TPS is ~5-15% of entry mass (general) frees roughly 1-4% of entry mass for payload or margin elsewhere. On a 20 t-payload human-class Mars lander with a ~16 m heat shield, that is plausibly 0.5-1 t (judgment). Commercial capsule makers are not bound by NASA margin policy, so the band is not capped. A NASA crewed adopter would be capped at Medium.
nodes.strongest_case_small: For small capsules TPS mass is small in absolute terms and reliability matters more. Post-Artemis I, NASA flagship and crewed programs will resist thinner margins.
nodes.signpost: A NASA EDL margin-policy update, or Varda or Inversion disclosing reliability-based TPS sizing or reduced TPS mass.

nodes.title: Validated supersonic-retropropulsion aero-propulsive models
nodes.description: Predictive models of plume-shock interaction, aerodynamic forces and moments, and heating during supersonic retropropulsion (SRP) for 20-100 t Mars landers, reduced to control-oriented models with quantified uncertainty and accepted by a lander program.
nodes.status_oct2026: NASA's EDL Architecture Study found that all its 20 t human-scale concepts need SRP. Large DES and CFD runs on leadership supercomputers are the main tool (general). Falcon 9 and Starship Earth-reentry burns are the only full-scale data, and they are proprietary.
nodes.why: Uncertainty in aero-propulsive interaction feeds GNC control margins and the propellant budget, and SRP propellant is a large share of landed mass (general). On-demand applied math turns expensive unsteady CFD campaigns into reduced-order models with uncertainty bounds. Validation needs flight data that only SpaceX holds at scale.
nodes.strongest_case_small: SpaceX will validate empirically through Earth flights and accept risk on early Mars attempts. NASA's human Mars EDL has no decision driver before 2031.
nodes.signpost: Published SRP models validated against Starship or Falcon flight data, or a NASA Mars architecture selecting a lander concept.

nodes.title: Formally verified entry, aerocapture and powered-descent guidance
nodes.description: Entry, aerocapture and powered-descent guidance (numerical predictor-corrector, convex powered-descent guidance) delivered with machine-checked proofs of convergence, constraint satisfaction and floating-point error bounds for the flight implementation, and accepted as verification evidence.
nodes.status_oct2026: Convex powered-descent guidance has pen-and-paper proofs (general). Flight code is verified by test and Monte Carlo. The release shows agentic Lean at scale for mathematics, not for flight code, and no tool is qualified.
nodes.why: Aerocapture allows a single pass, so a guidance failure means losing the mission. Proofs of robust convergence under atmospheric-density dispersions reduce Monte Carlo burden and perceived risk, and certification regimes already give credit for formal methods. Capped at Medium in S2 and S3 because acceptance is required.
nodes.strongest_case_small: Guidance mishaps have historically come from requirements, sensor and integration errors, not from algorithm convergence, and a proof of the wrong specification is worthless.
nodes.signpost: A NASA or commercial EDL flight-software release with formal proof artifacts accepted as verification evidence.

nodes.title: Coupled plasma-sheath and RF-link prediction tools
nodes.description: Coupled tools for nonequilibrium flowfield, electron density and full-wave electromagnetics that predict and minimize RF blackout through antenna placement, aft-side relay to constellations, and magnetic or electrostatic windows.
nodes.status_oct2026: Starship relays through Starlink during reentry. Magnetic-window theory is at the screening-model stage (Lieu, arXiv 2608.10018, Aug 2026). The reentry sheath is collisional and weakly ionized, so family 362 (collisionless relativistic Vlasov-Maxwell, T3) does not bear on it.
nodes.why: This is a coupled-physics analysis that is solved in principle but expert-scarce, so AI makes it routine for every vehicle. Better electron-density prediction also benefits from the ionization kinetics in the radiation node.
nodes.strongest_case_small: Relaying through the wake to Starlink already largely solves the operational problem. Magnetic windows need heavy, high-field magnets, so the practical impact is small.
nodes.signpost: A flight demonstration of active blackout mitigation, which would be a surprise before 2030.

nodes.title: Rapidly reusable orbital heat shield (ship scale)
nodes.description: One Starship-class orbital vehicle reflies at least 5 times, with heat-shield turnaround under ~2 weeks and tile replacement limited to a small fraction per flight.
nodes.status_oct2026: First orbital flight on 28 Sep 2026 (Flight 14, two orbits, early deorbit, splashdown). No ship has been caught or reflown. The tile stress test on Flight 13 showed cracking and gap streaks, and SpaceX publicly calls the heat-shield problem solved.
nodes.why: Ship catch, then reflight, then 5 reflights is a hardware-iteration sequence paced by flight count. Booster reuse took roughly 1-2 years from first catch to routine reflight (general). AI damage models and inspection theory remove some inspection labor and shorten learning by perhaps 6-12 months in S2 and S3 (judgment). They do not change the ceramic material or the flight clock, so the band does not move across scenarios.
nodes.strongest_case_small: SpaceX gets there through empirical hardware iteration, with or without AI mathematics. If the tile concept is a dead end for rapid reuse (Rasky), the fix is a new TPS architecture, a fabrication and qualification problem measured in years.
nodes.signpost: First ship catch and reflight (2027?), with published turnaround time and tile replacement counts.

nodes.title: Flown heat shield sized with reduced, model-based margins
nodes.description: A flown reentry capsule or planetary probe whose TPS was sized by probabilistic, model-based margins and is at least ~15% thinner than stacked-factor practice, with flight data confirming the bondline predictions.
nodes.status_oct2026: Commercial capsules fly every few months (Varda W-5 in Jan 2026, W-6 in 2026, with a Sandia instrumented nose tile). NASA's SRL study shows ~25% thinning is possible at 99% confidence.
nodes.why: This is the shortest chain in the domain from AI mathematics to flown hardware: AI-run UQ, then probabilistic sizing, then a commercial capsule iterating on a monthly-to-quarterly cadence with instrumented heat shields. It frees ~1-4% of entry mass (general) and turns each flight into a calibration point. P7 defaults to Speculative; the band is raised because commercial capsules iterate in months and need no certification body to accept margins.
nodes.strongest_case_small: Capsule makers may prefer to spend the margin on reliability and reuse rather than mass, so the change may be invisible from outside. Payload mass is rarely the binding constraint on small capsules.
nodes.signpost: A capsule operator reports flight-measured bondline temperatures matching pre-flight probabilistic predictions on a thinned heat shield.

nodes.title: First aerocapture flight demonstration
nodes.description: A vehicle uses a single atmospheric pass to capture into orbit (an Earth demonstration), validating the guidance, aerothermal and model-correlation performance that a planetary flagship would need before relying on aerocapture.
nodes.status_oct2026: Aerocapture has never flown. On 11 Sep 2026 Inversion received a $350k NASA purchase order to study an Arc-based Earth aerocapture demo, running through 30 Jun 2027 with NASA Ames support. Uranus studies find MSL-heritage aeroshells adequate but require a risk-reduction flight demo first.
nodes.why: In S2, AI collapses analysis cost (guidance design, dispersion analysis, aerothermal and rarefied analysis), so a small commercial vehicle could attempt the demo for tens of millions of dollars instead of as a NASA-class program. Funding and a ride bind. The earliest credible flight follows a 2027 study plus about 2 years of build.
nodes.strongest_case_small: Analysis cost was never the barrier; NASA funding is, and the planetary budget is under pressure. The study is only $350k.
nodes.signpost: NASA awards a flight contract for an aerocapture demo after the study ends in June 2027.

nodes.title: Ground-validated design basis for 12-14 km/s Earth return
nodes.description: A validated aerothermal environment (radiative plus convective) and TPS response model (HEEET-class 3D woven material) for crewed Mars-return or fast sample-return entries, with radiative uncertainty of 25% or less, accepted by a mission project.
nodes.status_oct2026: Earth entry at 12 km/s implies more than 3,000 W/cm2 and ~250 kPa (ESA). HEEET is designed for 1,500-8,000 W/cm2. Radiation becomes first-order above ~12 km/s. No funded mission needs this before 2031 (general).
nodes.why: Specific kinetic energy is ~72 MJ/kg at 12 km/s against ~30 MJ/kg from LEO, and radiation dominates. Radiative uncertainty sets material choice and thickness. AI-built kinetics could halve it, but without a mission to pull the work, nobody spends the shock-tube and arc-jet time.
nodes.strongest_case_small: No funded mission needs it before 2031. Ground facilities cannot replicate the combined environment, and flight tests at these speeds are extremely rare.
nodes.signpost: NASA or ESA selects a mission with Earth entry at 12 km/s or more and a radiative heating factor below 1.3.

nodes.title: Next deployable heat-shield flight (inflatable or mechanical, 10 m class or larger)
nodes.description: An orbital-entry flight of an inflatable (HIAD) or mechanically deployable (ADEPT) aeroshell of 10 m class or larger, the scale path toward the 16-18 m aeroshells studied for heavy Mars landers.
nodes.status_oct2026: LOFTID (6 m) flew in Nov 2022. No funded follow-on was found as of Oct 2026. NASA's EDL Architecture Study considered HIAD and ADEPT for 20 t Mars payloads.
nodes.why: Coupled fluid-structure-thermal behavior of flexible TPS (nonlinear membrane mechanics, flutter, fabric permeability) suits AI applied math well. Whether it flies depends on a budget line and a launch opportunity.
nodes.strongest_case_small: Starship's rigid-body approach to heavy Mars EDL may make deployables irrelevant for cargo, and no budget line exists.
nodes.signpost: NASA or ULA announces a LOFTID follow-on flight.

nodes.title: First landing of 20 t or more on Mars
nodes.description: A Starship-class or other vehicle lands 20 t or more intact on Mars, demonstrating heavy Mars EDL: entry at ~6-7.5 km/s, aerobraking, then retropropulsive descent.
nodes.status_oct2026: On 8 Feb 2026 Musk said SpaceX had shifted focus to a city on the Moon, with Mars to follow in roughly 5-7 years. The S-1 (20 May 2026) gives no Mars date. Starship reached orbit on 28 Sep 2026 and has not yet attempted propellant transfer. The late-2026 window is effectively not being used for a landing attempt (general inference).
nodes.why: The binding clock is the 26-month synodic window. Before end-2031 there are about two launch opportunities, around late 2028/early 2029 and around early 2031 (general), and propellant transfer, cryogenic storage and SpaceX's Moon priority come first. AI mathematics improves SRP and aerothermal models, plus margins (0.5-1 t on a 20 t-class lander, judgment), which raises the odds of a first attempt succeeding but cannot add windows. S3 is Medium only because S3 assumes AI accelerates engineering across the whole program, not just EDL.
nodes.strongest_case_small: AI mathematics has a near-nil effect on whether or when this happens. SpaceX's strategic choice and orbital refilling decide.
nodes.signpost: A SpaceX commitment to the late-2028 window, or the first ship-to-ship propellant transfer (2027?).

nodes.title: Point-to-point rocket cargo, repeated demonstration flights
nodes.description: At least 3 suborbital point-to-point flights deliver 30 t or more of cargo to remote landing sites, with the vehicle recovered, per the Space Force Point-to-Point Delivery (P2PD) concept.
nodes.status_oct2026: The 2022 DoD contract with SpaceX envisaged landing ~30 t of cargo in a 2026 test. The Johnston Atoll environmental assessment was suspended in July 2025. No demonstration as of Oct 2026.
nodes.why: Point-to-point needs a rapidly reusable ship that can land on land, range and overflight approvals, sonic-boom and environmental clearance, and host-nation landing rights. Of these, only the aerothermal design is cognitive, and it is already adequate. AI mathematics has essentially no effect on the regulatory and range gates.
nodes.strongest_case_small: The effect is nil. The program's fate turns on DoD priorities and SpaceX's manifest.
nodes.signpost: A new environmental assessment or range agreement for P2PD landing sites.

nodes.title: Routine, cheap reentry: 50+ commercial returns a year
nodes.description: Commercial capsule returns (in-space manufacturing, defense hypersonic testbeds, cargo) exceed ~50 a year worldwide, and TPS is no longer a pacing or major cost item.
nodes.status_oct2026: Varda flew two reentries by mid-2026 (W-5 in Jan, then W-6) and targets monthly. Inversion, The Exploration Company and others are developing capsules (general). Landing sites are limited, for example Koonibba in South Australia.
nodes.why: AI mathematics contributes at the margin: cheaper qualification by analysis for each new capsule variant, thinner and partly reusable TPS (+1-4% of entry mass), and faster design iterations. In S2 the AI-built aerothermal stack lets a 20-person company carry the analysis load of a NASA center. Demand for returned products, rideshare cadence and landing-site licensing are the real drivers.
nodes.strongest_case_small: Demand is unproven, TPS is already a small share of cost, and launch rideshare cadence and reentry licensing bind first.
nodes.signpost: A count of commercial reentries in 2028 above 20, with more than one operator.

nodes.title: Aerocapture baselined for an outer-planet flagship
nodes.description: NASA or ESA baselines aerocapture for a Uranus, Neptune or Titan orbiter, cutting cruise time by years and shifting propellant mass to science.
nodes.status_oct2026: The Uranus Orbiter and Probe baseline uses propulsive orbit insertion with a 13-15 year cruise. Aerocapture studies show faster Uranus orbiters are feasible but require a flight demo.
nodes.why: Aerocapture can cut cruise to Uranus by several years and save insertion propellant (Uranus aerocapture literature). AI-cheapened analysis, plus guidance that can be verified, lowers perceived risk. Still, a successful demo and a flagship budget decision must both land before 2031.
nodes.strongest_case_small: Pressure on NASA's planetary budget makes any new flagship baseline decision unlikely before 2031, whatever the technology.
nodes.signpost: A Uranus flagship study update that carries aerocapture as baseline rather than as an option.

scenario_contrast: Working assumption for the shared nodes (owned elsewhere): cap-research-math-public arrives in 2028 in S1 and 2027 in S2/S3; cap-applied-math in 2029/2027/2027; cap-physics-theory after 2031 in S1, 2029 in S2, 2028 in S3; cap-design-optimization 2031/2029/2028; cap-autonomous-labs after 2031, 2029, 2028; infra-mathlib-applied 2030/2028/2027; infra-verified-numerics after 2031, 2029, 2028; infra-tool-qualification after 2031, 2030, 2029. Moving from S1 to S2 shifts the domain's tier-2 nodes (stability analysis, test design, margin UQ, inverse NDE) 1-2 years earlier and up one band, because they are solved in principle but expert-scarce and only the cognitive clock binds. Tier-3 physics nodes (transition, SBLI closures, radiation kinetics, gas-surface chemistry, ablator response) move about 2 years in S2. They stay at Low or Medium because each needs physical calibration: arc-jet hours at what is NASA's only reentry TPS facility, EAST shock-tube shots, and a few transition flights a year. The flight-data node grows linearly, not exponentially, in every scenario. Tier 5-7 nodes barely move: rapid reuse and Mars landing are paced by flight count, synodic windows and SpaceX strategy, and point-to-point by regulation. The commercial-capsule chain (UQ, then probabilistic sizing, then a thinner flown TPS) is the one place where S2 turns into flown hardware before 2031, because capsules iterate every few months and need no certification body to accept margins. S3 adds autonomous experiments and AI-accelerated programs from ~2028, which helps materials and chemistry calibration and gives a small lift to whole-program outcomes such as the Mars landing (Low to Medium). It cannot create arc jets, launch windows or range approvals.
key_insights: The biggest near-term lever in entry systems is margins, not a theorem. NASA's own SRL study (IPPW 2026) shows a heat shield at ~75% of baseline thickness still meets 99% bondline-temperature confidence. Rigorous joint UQ is solved in principle but expert-scarce, the classic case where on-demand AI mathematics pays first (P1, then P5).

The domain is bound by validation data, not cognition. The arc jet (NASA's only reentry TPS facility), the EAST shock tube and a few transition flights a year set the slope. AI's highest-value early role is test design that maximizes information per run, multiplying the physical gate instead of pretending to bypass it.

Radiative heating is the largest physics gap for fast entries. At SRL's 8 km/s, baseline models under-predicted VUV by up to 2x against EAST, and UQ methods disagreed between 30% and 100% (Sep 2026). AI-built kinetics can plausibly halve that by 2030 in S2, but family 275 (T1) caps first-principles shortcuts and shock-tube time binds.

The openai/math catalog contributes little directly. Families 363 and 364 (T1) change confidence in DSMC and Boltzmann modeling; 365 (T3), 372 and 366 (T1) inform heat-shield inspection theory, with 365's conductivity nonuniqueness the most actionable as a P3 design rule (do not rely on thermal boundary data alone); 275 and 278 (T1) are ceilings on ab initio chemistry. None changes a heating number.

Starship rapid reuse and the first heavy Mars landing are paced by hardware and launch windows. AI mathematics shifts them by months at most, and only two Mars launch opportunities remain before end-2031 (about late 2028 and early 2031).

The fastest chain from AI mathematics to flown hardware runs through commercial capsules (Varda-class, flying every few months with instrumented heat shields): AI-run UQ, then probabilistic sizing, then thinner flown TPS, plausibly by 2029 in S2.
Formal verification reaches EDL through guidance software and numerics kernels, not aerothermal physics, and is capped by tool qualification (around 2030-31 even in S2).

In S2 the main structural change is that analysis stops being scarce. A small company can carry the analysis load of a NASA center (aerocapture demo, new capsules, deployables), but capital and launch access then become the gates.
nil_effects: Entry energy budget: ~30 MJ/kg from LEO, ~72 MJ/kg at 12 km/s. Physics fixes how much energy must be dissipated, so TPS cannot be designed away, only right-sized.

Ground-test capacity: no scenario builds new arc jets or shock tubes fast. The Ames Arc Jet Complex is NASA's only reentry TPS ground facility, and DoD calls hypersonic test capacity a national bottleneck. AI can only use the hours better.
Mars synodic windows: only two launch opportunities before end-2031. Cognition does not add windows.

Material capability: better theory does not make PICA, Avcoat or ceramic tiles better. New TPS materials need fabrication, arc-jet and flight qualification on a 5-10 year clock, though autonomous labs in S3 compress discovery but not qualification.
Galactic speedups: family 107 (matrix-multiplication exponent 9/4 or below) and family 130 (FFT below n log n) give no practical speedup to CFD, DSMC or radiation solvers.
Family 362 (relativistic Vlasov-Maxwell smoothness, T3) has no bearing on reentry plasma sheaths or blackout. The sheath is collisional, weakly ionized and non-relativistic.

Family 376 and the separate Sep 2026 forced Navier-Stokes blowup claim: forced-flow results say nothing about hypersonic heating, transition or turbulence closures, which remain closure-and-data problems.
Well-posedness results (363, 364, 362) change confidence in models, not predicted heat fluxes or TPS thickness.
Regulatory and range gates for point-to-point transport (overflight, sonic boom, landing-site environmental reviews, host-nation rights) and FAA reentry licensing are untouched.
Classified defense hypersonic flight data will not flow to civil model builders because of better mathematics, so civil model calibration stays data-poor.

signposts.event: Outside teams can buy research-grade math capability (OpenAI or another lab) by mid-2027
signposts.what_it_changes: Confirms S2 timing for all P1 nodes (stability analysis, test design, margin UQ, inverse NDE). If public access slips past 2028, shift these nodes one year later and down one band, toward S1.

signposts.event: Expert review or a Comparator check of families 363/364 (Boltzmann) and 365 (inverse problems) within 12 months
signposts.what_it_changes: Moves hyper-boltzmann-foundations-check to T2/T4 and settles whether the nonuniqueness is entropy-admissible. A refutation removes the kinetic catalog links but leaves the capability-driven nodes unchanged.

signposts.event: A NASA, ESA or commercial program adopts reliability-based TPS sizing (margin-policy revision, design-review citation, or a capsule operator disclosure)
signposts.what_it_changes: Confirms the margins chain (hyper-probabilistic-tps-sizing to hyper-thinner-tps-flown) and supports pulling the S2 flown date to 2028-29.

signposts.event: First Starship ship catch and reflight, with published heat-shield turnaround and tile-replacement counts (2027?)
signposts.what_it_changes: Sets the real data clock for hyper-tile-damage-accumulation and hyper-rapid-reuse-heatshield. A new TPS architecture announcement would push both out by years.

signposts.event: A blind or flight-validated AI-assisted transition prediction (BOLT-1B follow-ons, MACH-TB flights)
signposts.what_it_changes: Raises hyper-transition-prediction-theory from Low toward Medium in S2. Failure confirms the data gate dominates.

signposts.event: AI-generated radiation kinetics match EAST VUV spectra within 20% without tuning, at a radiation workshop or IPPW
signposts.what_it_changes: Raises hyper-radiation-kinetics and the 12+ km/s design basis. It would justify lowering radiative heating factors from ~1.5 toward ~1.25.

signposts.event: NASA awards an aerocapture flight demonstration after the Inversion study ends (June 2027)
signposts.what_it_changes: Makes hyper-aerocapture-demo Medium or better in S1. Without an award by 2028, all aerocapture outcome nodes stay Low or Speculative.

signposts.event: Mathlib or another proof library gains substantial PDE and numerical-analysis coverage (Sobolev spaces, finite-volume convergence, floating-point semantics) during 2027
signposts.what_it_changes: Pulls hyper-verified-aerothermal-numerics and hyper-certified-edl-guidance earlier. Slow coverage keeps them after 2031 in S1.

signposts.event: SpaceX commits a Starship to the late-2028 Mars window and demonstrates ship-to-ship propellant transfer
signposts.what_it_changes: Moves hyper-mars-heavy-landing from 2031 to 2029 in all scenarios. That would be a physical-clock change, not an AI-mathematics one.
